title: Oscar Wilde, The Picture of Dorian Gray recast
author: Salon
note: This whole-book remake includes murder, corruption, and a violent death. Period-true to Wilde’s ending, written without gore spectacle. Warn the room before you Host it; offer a midpoint pause if needed.

breaths.text: Bai Sheng painted in a top-floor studio above the Bund where Huangpu freight and ferry lights scored the glass.
The portrait on the easel was nearly finished: Du Yan at twenty, beauty so complete it made the room look provisional.
Bai worked as if the paint might refuse to dry into anything less than mercy.
Liu Heng arrived without knocking, cologne and curiosity preceding him.
He leaned on the sill and watched the river commerce like a man who believed cities existed to illustrate his epigrams.
Liu Heng: Your sitter has the face of a person who has not yet chosen a vice.
How exhausting for him.
Bai: Leave him alone, Liu Heng.
He is not one of your experiments.
Du Yan stepped down from the platform, smiling the way people smile when they have never been refused.
Shanghai had already forgiven his face in advance.
Bai introduced them with the reluctance of a man handing over a rare book.
Liu Heng spoke of youth as a temporary republic and beauty as the only aristocracy that did not require paperwork.
Du Yan listened as if hearing a language he had always half known.
When Bai covered the canvas for the day, Du Yan glanced once more at his own likeness and said, lightly, that it was a pity the painting could not stay young while he grew old.
He did not know he had spoken a contract.
They dined in the French Concession in a private room that smelled of citrus oil and expensive restraint.
Liu Heng’s doctrine arrived between courses: sensation as duty, morality as bad lighting, conscience as a provincial relative who stayed too long.
Du Yan: And if beauty is the only thing that matters, what happens when it leaves?
Liu Heng: It leaves.
That is the joke.
The clever live faster before the punchline.
Bai watched Du Yan’s face change under the talk the way a plant turns toward a brighter window.
Afterward, walking along Huaihai, Bai begged Du Yan not to see Liu Heng alone.
Du Yan laughed and promised nothing.
That night the finished portrait hung opposite Du Yan’s bed in his Huangpu apartment.
River humidity softened the varnish.
He looked from glass to canvas and wished again—clearer, hungrier—that the picture would bear every mark of age and sin while he remained untouched.
Something in the room seemed to agree.
He slept without dreaming and woke unmarked.
He found Su Yan in a theater off Fuxing Road where Shakespeare was performed for tourists and the lonely.
She was Juliet, Ophelia, Imogen by rotation; her talent made the cheap scenery irrelevant.
Du Yan went night after night.
When he met her backstage, she called him Prince Charming because his name felt too ordinary for the story she needed.
Su Yan: You watch as if the play were happening to you.
Du Yan: It is.
You make it happen.
They walked the Concession after curtain.
She spoke of art as rescue; he spoke of her as the only real thing in a city of surfaces.
He told Bai and Liu Heng he was engaged to an actress.
Bai worried.
Liu Heng applauded the experiment.
Then Su Yan, loving him, lost the art that had made her luminous.
On the night he brought his friends, she acted like a schoolgirl reading lines.
The audience shifted.
Liu Heng’s smile sharpened.
Afterward Du Yan found her radiant with private happiness and empty of craft.
Du Yan: You have killed my love.
Without your art you are nothing to me.
Su Yan: I have something better than art.
I have you.
He left her in the dressing room with greasepaint and ruin.
By morning she was dead—poison, the papers said, or grief made chemical.
Du Yan received the news with a strange calm.
When he looked at the portrait, the mouth had hardened into a cruelty he recognized as his own.
He showed Bai nothing.
He covered the portrait and moved it to the attic room above his apartment, locking the door.
Liu Heng sent a yellow-bound novel of French decadence; Du Yan read it as scripture.
Years began to pass in Shanghai’s glamorous weather: clubs along the Bund, private views in converted lane houses, opium dens dressed as tea rooms for men who still required a story.
The portrait aged.
A wrinkle here, a stain of appetite there.
Du Yan’s face in mirrors stayed the face Bai had loved.
Rumors attached themselves to his name—ruined protégés, vanished evenings, a married woman who left the city suddenly.
He smiled through them.
Beauty was still his passport.
Bai, returning from months abroad, found Du Yan unchanged and the city changed around him.
He pleaded for honesty.
Bai: They say terrible things.
Deny them for my sake.
Du Yan: Come upstairs.
In the attic the portrait waited: corrupt, sly, older than any man of Du Yan’s apparent years.
Bai stared until prayer failed him.
Bai: This is the face of your soul.
Good God, Du Yan—
Du Yan: You taught me to worship it.
Blame your own worship.
Rage arrived like a decision already made.
He stabbed Bai repeatedly with a knife kept for opening crates.
Bai’s blood darkened the floorboards.
The portrait’s hands gained a fresh red.
Du Yan stood breathing hard, still beautiful, already planning the disposal.
He blackmailed Kang Wei—chemist, once almost a friend—into destroying the body with acids and science.
Kang obeyed and later shot himself.
Du Yan returned to dinners.
Liu Heng noticed only that Du Yan seemed tired of being interesting.
Su Yan’s brother, Jian Yan, a sailor with a long memory, came hunting through Shanghai’s docks for the gentleman who had destroyed his sister.
He glimpsed Du Yan near the Custom House and mistook youth for innocence until an old woman in an alley named the face that never aged.
Jian tracked him to a shooting party upriver; a hunter’s accident killed Jian instead.
Du Yan felt relief so sharp it frightened him into a week of attempted goodness—charity, returned letters, refused invitations.
The portrait did not soften.
Hypocrisy, it seemed, stained worse than open vice.
On the eve of a gallery opening for which his unbroken beauty was half the draw, Du Yan stood before the canvas and understood that reform without confession was only another pose.
He seized the knife that had killed Bai.
Du Yan: Now you will die.
He drove the blade into the portrait.
A cry shook the building.
Servants broke the attic door at dawn and found, on the floor, a withered old man in evening clothes, knife in his heart, face lined with every sin the city had whispered.
On the wall, Bai Sheng’s portrait hung restored: Du Yan young, exquisite, unstained.
They identified the body by the rings on its fingers.
The Bund kept its schedule.
Ferries crossed.
Liu Heng, hearing the news over coffee, remarked that it was a pity—Du Yan had been the one person left in Shanghai who still looked like a theory come true.
Bai’s name rose briefly in obituaries and sank.
The portrait entered a private collection and was later said to have been lost in a warehouse fire near the river.
What remained was the story the painting had always told more honestly than the living face: that beauty without conscience is a loan, and Shanghai, like every glamorous city, collects.
Du Yan’s early weeks after the wish had been almost innocent—parties where he practiced Liu Heng’s sentences until they fit his mouth.
He learned which clubs photographed well and which required silence.
He discovered that people confessed to beauty as they confessed to priests.
A young collector from Hong Kong offered him a share in a shipping concern; Du Yan declined, preferring evenings that left no ledger.
Bai sent anxious notes.
Du Yan answered with invitations and never arrived on time.
Su Yan’s theater smelled of dust and orange peel.
Before the fatal night she had performed Rosalind with a brightness that made Du Yan believe love and art could share a body.
He bought her a bracelet from a jeweler on Nanjing Road and watched her turn it under the bulb as if it were proof of a future.
Her mother, shrewd and tired, asked what a gentleman intended.
Du Yan spoke of marriage with the sincerity of a man who had not yet tested sincerity against boredom.
Liu Heng: Marry her.
Or don’t.
Either way you will learn something vulgar about yourself.
The learning came when Su Yan’s talent collapsed into devotion.
Du Yan’s cruelty that night was precise because it felt aesthetic: he could not love a face that had stopped being a performance.
After her death he walked until dawn along the river and found, in the locked attic, that the portrait had taken the first installment—a cruelty around the mouth, a shadow under the eyes.
He laughed, then covered the canvas with a cloth that had once draped Bai’s model stand.
Years thickened.
He hosted dinners where conversation was a blood sport and left before dessert.
He funded a sculptor and ruined him with attention.
He kept a flat in a lane off Julu Road for evenings that required another address.
The yellow book Liu Heng had given him became a map; he followed it into rooms where time softened and faces blurred.
Always he returned to the attic to watch the portrait accept what his mirror refused.
Bai’s final visit was not an accident.
Bai had heard enough.
In the attic, confronted with the painted ledger of Du Yan’s life, Bai wept for the boy he had immortalized and for his own complicity in that immortality.
Du Yan’s murder was not rage alone; it was the panic of a man whose secret had grown a body.
When Kang Wei’s science erased Bai from the floor, Du Yan wiped the knife and went to a concert at the Conservatory as if culture could bleach the afternoon.
Jian Yan’s pursuit threaded the docks with a simpler morality: a sister dead, a gentleman to blame.
Du Yan’s unchanged face nearly saved him until folklore—Shanghai’s gossip in an older register—named the devil who did not age.
Jian’s death in the upriver accident felt to Du Yan like luck, and luck felt like permission.
He tried kindness as a costume.
The portrait sneered through varnish.
On the last night he dressed for the gallery as if beauty were still an argument.
Alone with the canvas he understood that the only remaining honesty was destruction.
The knife entered paint and found flesh.
Morning’s servants found the accounting complete: youth restored to oil, age and crime returned to the man who had borrowed against his soul.
Liu Heng would dine out on the irony for a season.
The Huangpu would take no notice.
In a city that sold faces as currency, Du Yan had spent every coin and discovered, too late, that the portrait had been the bank.
He had not always been monstrous.
In the first months he still visited Bai’s studio, still sat for small studies, still let Bai believe influence could be rationed.
Liu Heng’s friendship was a climate: witty, dry, impossible to leave without noticing how damp ordinary air had become.
At a charity ball in a Bund bank’s marble hall Du Yan danced with a diplomat’s daughter and forgot her name before the car arrived.
He told himself forgetting was elegance.
Su Yan’s dressing room after the ruined performance smelled of sweat and crushed flowers.
She reached for him; he stepped back as if from a stain.
Later he would tell Liu Heng he had been defending art.
Liu Heng would reply that art needed no defense from love—only from sincerity.
The line pleased Du Yan enough to live inside for years.
When he first locked the attic he placed a mirror opposite the covered portrait and practiced smiling until the smile looked inherited rather than learned.
Servants were told the room held family papers.
Once a cleaner found the door ajar and glimpsed a corner of canvas; Du Yan dismissed her with a month’s wages and a reference that ensured silence.
Shanghai’s service economy understood purchase.
Corruption preferred company.
He collected young men who wanted introductions and taught them Liu Heng’s doctrines until they could wound themselves without help.
A painter from Hangzhou hanged himself after a season in Du Yan’s circle; the portrait gained a tightness around the eyes.
Du Yan sent flowers to the funeral and was photographed looking grave.
Bai’s murder left a smell the chemicals could not entirely erase.
Du Yan burned Bai’s coat and watch in a stove and kept a sketch Bai had made of him at nineteen—proof, he told himself, of affection.
He slept poorly.
Liu Heng prescribed a week in Hangzhou’s tea hills; Du Yan went and returned no better, only better dressed.
Jian Yan’s face in the Custom House crowd had been Su Yan’s face made hard by labor.
For an instant Du Yan felt something like fear of justice.
Then he remembered his own reflection and walked on.
When news of Jian’s death reached him at a dinner, he excused himself to the terrace and watched container lights crawl the river like a rosary for the unrepentant.
The knife’s last work was almost tender.
He apologized to the portrait as one apologizes to a creditor.
The scream that followed was his own youth ending.
Identification by rings was bureaucratic mercy: beauty had finally become evidence.
In the years after, guides on the Bund sometimes pointed at Bai’s old studio building and told a shortened legend.
Tourists photographed the facade.
None of them looked for a soul in the paint.
That was the city’s final joke, and Wilde’s: the picture had always been the only honest face in the room.
Between Su Yan’s death and Bai’s murder the calendar did not dramatize itself.
It simply accrued.
Du Yan learned the difference between scandal that entertained and scandal that exiled.
He kept to the first by remaining beautiful and solvent.
Invitations continued.
Mothers who warned daughters still seated him near the orchids.
He bought a second apartment facing the river for no reason except that the view made loneliness look curated.
He filled it with lacquer, French novels, and a piano he did not play.
Friends came to be seen leaving.
Liu Heng came to talk.
Bai came less and less, then went abroad with a commission and a hope that distance might restore the boy in the portrait of his memory.
Du Yan’s cruelty refined.
He did not shout; he withdrew heat.
A young curator who loved him waited through a winter of almosts and then left for Beijing with a letter Du Yan never answered.
The portrait’s left cheek hollowed as if appetite had chewed from inside.
Du Yan touched his own face in the bathroom glass and found it smooth as a salesman’s promise.
Opium in Shanghai in those years wore good lighting.
In a house behind a pharmacy near the old town, Du Yan lay on clean mats and watched smoke invent architectures.
He woke with ideas for parties and debts he did not owe.
Once he dreamed Su Yan alive and speaking in perfect verse; he woke angry at the dream for being better than his memory.
Liu Heng: You are becoming a myth about yourself.
Myths are so difficult to divorce.
Du Yan: Then I shall stay married to mine.
They laughed.
Under the laugh Du Yan heard the attic door.
Kang Wei had loved Du Yan once in the careful way of men who fear newspapers.
When Du Yan summoned him after the murder, that old love became a lever.
Kang’s hands shook over the chemicals; Du Yan’s did not.
Afterward Kang said he would never speak to him again.
Du Yan agreed as if granting a favor.
Weeks later the shot in Kang’s laboratory was reported as accident.
Du Yan sent no flowers.
The gallery week that ended him had been meant as rehabilitation theater: Du Yan, still young, still collecting, still proof that Shanghai rewarded surface.
He had planned to hang lesser works and stand among them like a living caption.
Instead he climbed to the attic with the knife and closed the account.
Servants testified to a cry.
Police noted the aged corpse and the young painting and preferred not to write theology into the report.
Liu Heng, informed at the Club, ordered another coffee and said that nature had a vulgar taste for endings.
What Shanghai kept was simpler: a story about a face that would not pay its debts until the last morning, when the portrait—Bai’s love made durable—gave the debt back with interest.
After the portrait first changed, Du Yan tested the bargain like a scientist with a dangerous sample.
He said a cutting thing to a waiter and checked the canvas: a minute hardness at the lip.
He stayed out until the river light turned commercial and returned to find a shadow of fatigue painted under one eye while his own skin slept unmarked.
The experiment thrilled him more than any lover.
He began to keep the attic key on a chain against his chest.
On nights of excess he visited the painting as penitents visit relics, except his pilgrimage was triumph.
Look, he told the canvas, look what you carry for me.
The canvas looked back with an intelligence Bai had never intended.
Bai’s letters from abroad described light in other cities and asked after Du Yan’s health with the anxiety of a man who senses a door closing.
Du Yan replied with photographs of himself at openings—proof of wellness, proof of stasis.
Bai wrote that the photographs unsettled him.
Du Yan did not ask why.
Su Yan’s mother once waited outside his building.
He had her turned away with money.
The portrait’s hands yellowed as if nicotine and guilt shared a pigment.
He scrubbed his own hands until the soap burned and still felt clean.
In the final year before the murder he grew bored of vice that required other people.
He walked alone through the Concession at hours when delivery vans owned the streets.
He stood on the Bund and watched fog erase towers and return them.
He wondered whether Liu Heng had ever wished a portrait to age for him, and decided Liu Heng’s genius was to need no magic—only sentences.
When Bai returned and climbed those attic stairs, Du Yan felt almost grateful.
Confession would be forced; murder would be cleaner than speech.
The knife made the choice for both of them.
Years later a dealer claimed to have found Bai Sheng’s last portrait of Du Yan in a storage unit near Waigaoqiao.
Experts disputed provenance.
Collectors bid anyway.
The winning buyer hung it in a private room and never invited guests to see it.
Some bargains, even secondhand, prefer the dark.
The night Su Yan died, Du Yan did not go to the police station or the morgue.
He went home and uncovered the portrait by lamplight.
The change was small and absolute: the mouth had learned contempt.
He touched the painted lip and found only oil.
His own mouth in the dressing mirror remained soft, almost kind.
He poured wine and drank until the river’s noise became abstract.
Liu Heng arrived the next afternoon with newspapers and a theory.
Liu Heng: The poor girl has solved her reviews permanently.
You look astonishingly well for a widower of twenty-four hours.
Du Yan: We were not married.
Liu Heng: Precisely.
Tragedy without paperwork is so much cleaner.
Bai came later, gray with sympathy, and found Du Yan arranging flowers as if for a photograph.
Bai spoke of guilt; Du Yan spoke of art’s right to discard failed instruments.
Bai left unconvinced and newly afraid.
In the weeks that followed, Du Yan visited the attic daily.
Each minor sin—a lie to a creditor, a seduction performed as sport, a servant dismissed for seeing too much—registered on the canvas with bureaucratic patience.
He began to feel affection for the painting the way gamblers feel affection for the table that ruins them.
He returned once to Su Yan’s theater.
A different Juliet spoke the balcony lines without danger.
Du Yan sat in the dark and understood that his love had been for a temperature, not a person.
The portrait, that night, took a yellowish tone around the eyes, as if jaundice and knowledge shared a palette.
Liu Heng’s house off Wukang Road held books, cigarettes, and young people who wanted to be ruined stylishly.
Du Yan became the illustration of Liu Heng’s talk: proof that beauty could outrun consequence.
Women left marriages for a season of his attention and returned to their husbands with nothing actionable.
Men imitated his clothes and his cruelty and called it modernity.
Bai, painting less, wrote an essay on portraiture that never named Du Yan and somehow named only him.
Dealers asked Bai for another Du Yan.
Bai refused.
Du Yan sent champagne.
Bai did not drink it.
One autumn Du Yan traveled to Suzhou with a married collector and returned alone.
Gossip preferred not to specify.
The portrait’s hairline receded a fraction while Du Yan’s remained a brochure for youth.
He laughed in the attic until laughter sounded like someone else.
He kept Su Yan’s bracelet in a drawer and never wore it.
Once, drunk, he nearly threw it in the Huangpu; instead he locked it beside the attic key.
Relics, he decided, were for people who still believed in shrines.
When Bai came back from Europe he looked older in the honest way.
Du Yan received him in the riverside flat among orchids and denied every rumor with a smile that could have sold insurance.
Bai: There is a story about a boy in Hankou.
There is a story about a woman in the Concession.
There is a story about you that does not match your face.
Du Yan: Faces are poor evidence.
Bai: Then show me your soul.
The climb to the attic was short.
The unveiling was not.
Bai saw the painted ledger—vice, age, blood-hint, appetite—and fell to his knees as if beauty’s opposite required worship too.
Bai: What have you done with my Du Yan?
Du Yan: I kept him.
You only painted him.
The knife was where it always was.
Du Yan used it without speech after Bai began to pray.
Prayer felt like accusation.
When it was finished, Du Yan wiped his hands on Bai’s scarf and checked the portrait: fresh scarlet on the painted fingers.
He nodded as if at a correct receipt.
Kang Wei arrived before midnight.
Du Yan did not threaten with violence; he threatened with memory—letters, photographs, a summer Kang could not survive in daylight.
Kang worked until the body was chemistry.
At the door he said Du Yan had destroyed two men in one night.
Du Yan corrected him: one man and one inconvenience.
Jian Yan’s search gave the plot a simpler grammar.
He asked along the docks for a gentleman called Prince Charming.
He found enough to wait outside theaters and clubs.

The afternoon he seized Du Yan near the Custom House, Du Yan’s unchanged face made Jian release him—until an old woman from Su Yan’s neighborhood spat the truth: that face had worn years it refused to show.
Jian’s eyes changed.
Du Yan fled into traffic and privilege.
Fear made Du Yan almost good.
He funded a clinic.
He wrote an apology he did not send.
He refused an invitation that would have required someone else’s marriage to bend.
Then he checked the portrait and found hypocrisy uglier than crime.
Goodness as costume, the painting suggested, was the worst pigment of all.
The upriver shoot came as Liu Heng’s idea of fresh air.
Jian Yan appeared in the brake; a nervous gun discharged; Jian died in wet reeds.
Du Yan’s relief disgusted even him.
He returned to Shanghai determined to change in earnest and discovered he no longer knew what earnest meant.
The night before the opening he stood long before the canvas.
Bai’s murdered attention still lived in the brushwork beneath the corruption.
Du Yan spoke aloud.
Du Yan: If I destroy you, am I free—or only finished?
The portrait offered no epigram.
That had always been Liu Heng’s job.
Du Yan drove the knife in.
Pain found him at last: every deferred year, every outsourced line.
He fell.
Morning’s light—honest, bureaucratic—found an old dead man and a young restored painting.
Liu Heng heard at noon.
He said it was the first time Du Yan had been late for his own myth.
Then he asked who would inherit the apartment.
Even elegy, in Shanghai, required an address.
The servants who found the body never liked to tell the story complete.
They mentioned rings.
They mentioned the beautiful picture.
They omitted the smell of a life returned all at once.
Outside, the Bund performed another profitable day.
Inside, Wilde’s accounting closed: the face that would not pay had paid in full, and the art—Bai’s stubborn love—hung clean above the ruin.
Before Su Yan, before the attic lock, there was only Bai’s studio and Liu Heng’s voice and a young man who mistook attention for destiny.
Du Yan sat for hours while Bai negotiated light against the Bund’s glare.
Below them, porters shouted; above them, pigeons argued on the ledge.
Bai talked little when painting.
Liu Heng talked enough for both.
Liu Heng: People say they want to be good.
What they want is to be admired for the effort.
Du Yan: And what do you want?
Liu Heng: To be quoted accurately.
Bai scowled without looking away from the mouth he was refining.
He loved Du Yan with a painter’s panic—afraid that finishing the canvas would finish the feeling.
When the portrait was done, Bai’s hands shook.
Du Yan kissed his cheek with theatrical gratitude and looked past him toward Liu Heng for the real verdict.
That evening the three of them walked the Bund’s upper promenade.
Neon had begun its takeover of older signage; cranes stood like unfinished sentences over Pudong.
Du Yan felt newly invented.
He told them he would live as if youth were a politics.
Bai asked him to live as if friendship were one.
Liu Heng suggested politics bored him except as metaphor.
At home Du Yan hung the portrait and spoke his wish a third time, no longer lightly.
The room seemed to lean in.
He slept.
In the morning his face was the same and the painting—he could have sworn—looked slightly more tired around the eyes, as if it had stayed awake for him.
He spent the next days testing small cruelties: a canceled lunch, a borrowed idea claimed as his, a smile withheld from Bai at a crowded opening.
Each time the canvas took a mark.
Each time the mirror refused.
The bargain was no longer metaphor.
It was infrastructure.
Kang’s suicide—if suicide was the word the lab preferred—left Du Yan with a practical problem: fewer people who could be forced into intimacy with his secrets.
He became more careful and more reckless at once.
Careful in correspondence; reckless in appetite.
He hosted a masked dinner in a French Concession villa where no one used real names and everyone used real bodies.
At dawn he walked home past lane houses still shut and felt immortal in the stupid way of the uncaught.
He dreamed of Bai speaking from the floorboards.
He woke and opened windows until the river air scrubbed the room.
The portrait’s expression had grown sly.
Du Yan considered burning it and knew he would not.
Destroying the ledger would not destroy the debt; it would only destroy the proof that someone else was paying.
Jian Yan’s death should have ended fear.
Instead it taught Du Yan that luck was not absolution.
He sat through a charity concert for flood relief and donated conspicuously.
Photographers loved him.
The attic, later, loved him less: the painted face wore a sanctimonious twist that made Du Yan physically sick.
He threw a cloth over it and drank until the sickness became abstract again.
On the last afternoon he visited Bai’s old studio building.
New tenants made industrial furniture.
No one remembered the painter.
Du Yan stood on the stair and smelled, impossibly, turpentine and Bai’s soap.
He left before nostalgia became confession.
Liu Heng texted an invitation to supper.
Du Yan answered that he would come after the gallery preview.
He did not come.
He went upstairs with the knife and finished the only true autobiography Shanghai would ever have of him—written in oil, paid in flesh.
The police report remained thin.
Beauty confused procedure.
The restored portrait confused it more.
In private, one detective said the old dead man had the young man’s rings and the young man’s rooms and somehow not the young man’s face.
His partner told him to write what could be filed.
Years on, Liu Heng still told the story as an anecdote about wishing too precisely.
He never admitted he had taught the wish its vocabulary.
Bai was remembered by a handful of canvases in storage.
Du Yan was remembered as a face that had refused to learn time—until time, with a knife’s help, collected every lesson in a single night above the Huangpu.
Coda — What the city kept Shanghai did not moralize.
It filed.
The apartment was sold.
The attic was renovated into a closet for seasonal clothes.
A new tenant complained of a stain that would not leave the floorboards; workmen sanded and sealed until the wood looked innocent.
Innocence, in real estate, is a finish.
Somewhere a private collector still owns Bai Sheng’s portrait of Du Yan—or owns a convincing lie about it.
Guests who glimpse it say the boy’s beauty feels like an argument mid-sentence.
They do not know the sentence’s end.
That is as close as the market comes to mercy.
Liu Heng lived long enough to become a quotation without a source.
On slow afternoons he walked the Bund and imagined Du Yan beside him, still young, still listening.
The fantasy was Liu Heng’s last vanity: that influence could outlive the influenced.
In truth the portrait had been the only student who took perfect notes.
As for Du Yan—his name surfaced in club stories and vanished.
A few aging socialites claimed they had danced with him and that his hand had been cold.
Others insisted he had been kinder than rumor.
Kindness and coldness could both be true in a life that outsourced its reflection.
The knife had simply merged the books.
If there is a moral, Wilde already wrote it and Shanghai only translated it into river light and apartment keys: the soul will hang somewhere.
Choose the frame carefully.
Pay attention when the paint begins to look more honest than your face.
And when you reach for a weapon against your own ledger, understand you are not ending a picture.
You are calling due every hour you borrowed against a beauty that was never free.
One more inventory, for the record: Du Yan’s uncle’s allowance had funded the first years; later Du Yan’s own investments in river shipping and a quiet stake in a Concession gallery funded the rest.
Money made the bargain comfortable.
Without money the portrait might have been found earlier—poverty is a detective.
Wealth drew curtains.
He once almost confessed to a priest in a church near Xintiandi, more for the architecture than the sacrament.
He stood in the aisle, rehearsed a sentence about a painting, and left.
Outside, tourists photographed brick.
He photographed nothing.
His life was already being painted elsewhere.
On the morning after his death, a cleaner found Su Yan’s bracelet in a drawer and slipped it into her pocket before the police sealed the rooms.
She sold it months later in a market without knowing its story.
The bracelet outlived every principal.
Objects are patient that way.
Stories are less so—unless someone writes them down and refuses, this time, to rename the people who lived them.
Bai’s sister, years after, petitioned quietly for news of her brother’s last days in Shanghai.
Officials offered shrugs.
Liu Heng offered lunch and anecdotes that made Bai sound like a charming footnote to Du Yan’s legend.
She left the lunch untouched and walked the Bund alone, looking up at windows that did not look back.
She did not find the portrait.
She found only the city’s gift for absorbing unfinished grief into commerce.
And so the recast ends where Wilde ended: not with a sermon but with a recognition scene.
Youth on the wall.
Age on the floor.
The knife between them like a signature.
Call it magic if you need a genre.
Call it conscience if you need a moral.
Shanghai, glamorous and exacting in 2026’s hard light, simply calls it what happened—and keeps the ferries running while the story finds its next listener.
Du Yan’s name, when it surfaces now, surfaces with Bai Sheng’s and Liu Heng’s and Su Yan’s—together, as they must.
The portrait bargain only makes sense if the painter, the tempter, the actress, and the beautiful boy keep their own names in the city’s mouth.
